analysis.one_liner: Opens the entire Outer Continental Shelf and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its July 24, 2008 introduction it was sent to three House committees and never moved again, dying when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have erased every federal law barring oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and across the entire Outer Continental Shelf — the waters off America's coasts — and revoked presidential withdrawals of offshore areas. It then would have required the Interior Department to inventory oil and gas in those areas and write a five-year plan for lease sales, with 37.5 percent of new lease revenue going to Alaska and other coastal states, 25 percent to a new Department of Energy fund for clean-energy research, and the rest to the Treasury and conservation programs. It was introduced during the 2008 gasoline price spike, when expanded drilling was a major political issue.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: the bill hands them access to essentially all untapped federal offshore waters and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, creates a mandated federal inventory and five-year leasing plan to get them drilling quickly, and shares 37.5 percent of the resulting federal lease revenue with Alaska and other coastal states. A smaller slice of the public benefits through the clean-energy fund and the Land and Water Conservation Fund, but both depend on Congress actually appropriating the money later.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies seeking new federal leases

how_it_helps.text: It wipes out every federal legal prohibition on leasing the Outer Continental Shelf and ANWR for oil and gas, and revokes presidential withdrawals of offshore areas, making the entire coastline and the refuge available for lease sales.
It orders the Interior Department to inventory oil and gas across all these areas and write a five-year plan for lease sales, starting the leasing pipeline immediately.

It splits new lease revenues: 37.5 percent to Alaska and other coastal states, 25 percent to a new Department of Energy Reserve Fund for clean energy research, 25 percent to the Treasury, and 12.5 percent to the Land and Water Conservation Fund.

analysis.who_pays: The public owns these lands and waters, and bears the environmental cost: drilling industrializes coastal areas, adds spill risk to fishing and tourism economies, and permanently develops the Arctic Refuge. Taxpayers also give up part of the lease revenue stream — 37.5 percent would flow to state governments instead of the federal treasury. Motorists get no guaranteed price relief, since new leases take years to produce oil.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal communities, the Arctic Refuge, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill strikes down protections for the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the entire Outer Continental Shelf at once, opening coastal waters and protected wilderness to drilling rigs, spills, and industrial infrastructure with no area-by-area review.

Any price relief would come late: offshore and Arctic leases take years, often a decade or more, to move from lease sale to production, so the bill would not lower gasoline prices in the short term even if it raised eventual supply.

The clean-energy fund is contingent: it gets a quarter of new lease revenues and can only be spent if future appropriations acts and subsequent legislation authorize it, so the 'clean energy' half of the bill could easily never materialize.
The revenue-sharing formula sends 37.5 percent of new federal lease collections to Alaska and other coastal states, shrinking the federal and general public share of what is, by law, public oil.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill was the 2008 gas-price crisis and the argument that known oil under federal lands and waters was going untapped. The case against is stronger on its own terms: new leases would take years to produce oil, so near-term pump relief would be minimal; the oil belongs to the public, and the bill hands the main new stream of lease revenue to the industry and to producing states while the clean-energy fund is left to future Congresses; and the environmental and coastal risks are permanent while the supply effect is modest. As a bargain, it trades lasting public resources for uncertain and distant price relief, with the gains concentrated on leaseholders.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2008, referred to three House committees the same day, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Lampson introduced the bill on July 24, 2008, during a summer of record gasoline prices when expanded domestic drilling was a live national debate.

The same day it was referred to the Natural Resources, Science and Technology, and Energy and Commerce committees, and then to their Energy and Mineral Resources, Energy and Environment, and Energy and Air Quality subcommittees.

No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action is the July 28, 2008 subcommittee referral, and the bill expired with the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Arctic Refuge and protected offshore waters stayed closed to leasing, and coastal communities and everyone who values those public lands avoided the drilling the bill would have allowed; the oil industry lost a chance at new federal leases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Protected lands and coastal communities stayed off-limits to drilling

for.name: Rep. Nick Lampson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Domestic Drilling Act on July 24, 2008, to end all federal prohibitions on offshore and ANWR oil and gas leasing.

against.name: House Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Science and Technology Committees
against.role: Committees of referral, chaired by members of the House Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote is recorded; the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan bloc ever took a position on it; its sponsor was a Democrat at a time when expanded drilling was more often pressed by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill opens the entire Outer Continental Shelf and ANWR to leasing, creating a new supply of drillable federal acreage for companies that hold or would win the leases. The oil beneath those lands and waters belongs to the public; the bill's structure routes the main new revenue to leaseholders and to producing states.

industries.industry: Oil and gas leasing services (geophysical surveyors and drilling contractors)
industries.note: The mandated two-year resource inventory and five-year leasing plan would generate surveying, exploration, and contract work across newly opened federal waters and the refuge.

A new Department of Energy Reserve Fund is earmarked for clean-energy research, funded by 25 percent of new lease revenues — but the fund can only be spent through later appropriations acts, so the support is speculative rather than guaranteed.

New offshore drilling along the Outer Continental Shelf would put drilling infrastructure and spill risk in waters that fishing and beach-tourism businesses depend on; those industries had no seat in the bill, which opens all of the coast by statute.
